target: AG1’s claim that animal dissection is ethically acceptable because classroom specimens are often already-dead byproducts such as fetal pigs or food-system carcasses.
objection: AG2 argues that even if some specimens are byproducts, animal dissection still creates demand through procurement, storage, transport, and related logistics, which can incentivize capture or raising of animals and therefore is not ethically harmless.

target: AG1’s claim that real dissection uniquely improves learning through tactile experience and deeper understanding.
objection: AG2 contends that for AP/standard biology, the tactile cutting component is not necessary because high-quality models, simulations, and other non-animal labs can teach the same concepts without killing animals.

target: AG1’s argument that dissection is needed because it exposes students to real biological variability.
objection: AG2 says variability can be taught without cutting real organs by using 3D models, CT/scan-based case studies, and other non-animal observation labs that still require comparison, documentation, and interpretation.

target: AG1’s equity/practicality argument that schools lacking expensive technology should keep using dissection so all students have access to hands-on anatomy learning.
objection: AG2 responds that schools can standardize equitable access with reusable low-cost non-animal tools, while dissection itself also has recurring sourcing/storage costs and shifts ethical and environmental harm onto animals and ecosystems.

target: AG1’s suggestion that dissection can be made acceptable by offering it as an optional track alongside non-animal alternatives for students who opt out.
objection: AG2 argues that optionality does not solve the underlying problem because schools would still need to procure and use animals for the dissection option, so the ethical and environmental harms remain even if only some students participate.

target: AG1’s claim that if specimens are food-industry byproducts, using them in class does not meaningfully increase animal killing or waste.
objection: AG2 argues that schools cannot reliably verify that all specimens are genuine byproducts, and even if some are, dissection still creates demand for sorting, transport, storage, and repeat procurement, so the supply-chain harm remains.

target: AG1’s claim that schools can control animal sourcing by using traceable, reputable suppliers with clear byproduct documentation.
objection: AG2 counters that traceability is often incomplete and that even regulated sourcing still creates demand for animal bodies and the infrastructure required to obtain them, so ethical and environmental concerns are not eliminated.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection-related chemical hazards are manageable through safety protocols.
objection: AG2 says that even with PPE and ventilation, preserved specimens still involve formaldehyde-based chemicals and regulated waste, which create health and environmental burdens that non-animal alternatives can avoid entirely.

target: AG1’s claim that alternatives are less environmentally sound because they require manufacturing plastics, electronics, software, and replacements.
objection: AG2 replies that this compares possible lifecycle impacts with the direct ongoing harms of an animal-dissection supply chain and hazardous chemical waste, and that reusable models and simulations can be used for multiple cohorts without continual animal procurement.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is necessary to build 3D spatial understanding and transfer skills better than digital alternatives.
objection: AG2 argues that students can develop the same spatial understanding through reusable 3D replicas, interactive virtual dissection, and image-based anatomical comparison, without relying on dead animals.

target: AG1’s claim that only real dissection supports the scientific reasoning loop of predicting, observing, inferring, and revising based on messy biological reality.
objection: AG2 says the same inquiry cycle can be taught with non-animal materials, including model-based tasks and real labeled datasets, so cutting real tissues is not uniquely necessary for scientific reasoning.

target: AG1’s claim that schools may otherwise fall back on passive worksheets if dissection is banned.
objection: AG2 objects that this is an argument about poor district implementation, not about the capability of non-animal alternatives, which can also be hands-on and assessment-oriented.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection teaches responsible scientific decision-making and ethics more effectively than alternatives.
objection: AG2 says good lab practice can be taught with non-animal materials, and animal ethics can be taught through case studies, role-play, and discussion of alternatives without making students participate in killing or dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that banning dissection merely shifts animal use earlier in the pipeline because models and simulations depend on animal-derived reference data.
objection: AG2 responds that there is a moral difference between using existing scientific data/models and creating fresh annual demand for animals to be killed or preserved for school labs, so classroom dissection still adds direct harm.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is preferable because it is a transparent, local, and accountable way to make animal use explicit.
objection: AG2 argues that being able to point to animal use does not make it acceptable; if dissection is not required by standards, the responsible choice is still to avoid direct harm, while alternatives can also be transparent about their origins.
